reconcile.connective: Clarke reads the Hebrew מת ('dead') as a participle meaning 'dying,' letting Josiah die only after reaching Jerusalem, as Chronicles states.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptics Annotated Bible presses the point bluntly: Kings has him dead at Megiddo; Chronicles has him dying in Jerusalem.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Where did Josiah die?"
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Where did Josiah die?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Dead from Megiddo - The word מת meth should here be considered as a participle, dying, for it is certain he was not dead: he was mortally wounded at Megiddo, was carried in a dying state to Jerusalem, and there he died and was buried.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the Kings/Chronicles death-location tension by reinterpreting 'dead' at 2 Kings 23:30 as 'dying,' aligning Kings with Chronicles' account of Josiah dying only after reaching Jerusalem.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the Megiddo/Jerusalem question directly, arguing that the Hebrew meth ('dead') at 2 Kings 23:30 is better read as a participle, 'dying,' so Josiah died only after reaching Jerusalem as Chronicles states (per the 1977 Baker reprint, p. 376) — the same grammatical argument surfaced here from Adam Clarke's earlier commentary.

link.title: 2 Kings 23:30—Did Josiah die at Megiddo or at Jerusalem?
link.note: live apologetic treatment arguing Kings and Chronicles describe the same sequence: mortally wounded at Megiddo, died only after being carried to Jerusalem
